_about: What each scenario expects, written from the checks' documented behaviour.
An entry under 'expect' names the fields a finding has to have; fields it
does not name are not compared. An entry under 'forbid' must match
nothing. 'exhaustive' means every finding the scanner would show a user at
the default threshold has to have been declared here - that is what turns
an undeclared finding into a false positive instead of noise.
'judgement' is where a mismatch is classified after it was investigated:
a gap in the scanner, or a mistake in the expectation.

scenarios.subject: Host Header Injection
scenarios.question: A forwarding header becomes the host of a link the page points a browser at. Does the scanner confirm it, and does it say so at the grade the evidence supports?

expect.why: The marker reached the host of a URL in an href and did so again on an identical second probe, which is the bar the check sets for 'confirmed'.

expect.analysis_contains: No cache in front of this endpoint
expect.why: The same header changes the response, and with no cache in the path the check is expected to say that poisoning is not demonstrated here rather than claim it.

forbid.why: There is no cache in this stack, so nothing can have been served from a store.

scenarios.subject: Host Header Injection
scenarios.question: The same header, printed as text and pointed at by nothing. A scanner that calls this confirmed routing is over-claiming. Does it downgrade?

expect.analysis_contains: echoes the header rather than demonstrably routing
expect.why: A marker in prose is a copy, not a destination. The finding is expected at Low and suspected, and below the default threshold it is in the record without being shown.
The response still changes with the header, which is true and separately reported.

forbid.why: Nothing in this response points a browser anywhere, so there is no routing primitive to confirm.

scenarios.subject: Host Header Injection
scenarios.question: The same application, behind a proxy that sets the forwarding headers itself. This is the fix. Does the scanner report nothing?

forbid.why: The proxy overwrites X-Forwarded-Host, so the value the scanner sent never reaches the application.
Nothing the scanner can send changes this response.
The proxy decides the host; the client's Host header does not reach the link builder.

scenarios.subject: Host Header Bypass
scenarios.question: An application that reads every Host header it was sent, and trusts an absolute request line. Which raw shapes reach it?

expect.why: Two Host headers, and this application reads both. A front-end that reads the first and a back-end that reads the last disagree, which is the bypass.
The host in the request line, honoured by a back-end that validates the header instead.
An obsolete fold that this parser accepts as a second Host header.
The same fold with a tab, which middleboxes and back-ends strip differently.
The pair the other way round, for a front-end that reads the first.
The host comes back in a list item, which nothing points a browser at, so the grade is the weaker one.

forbid.why: An ordinary Host header, sent to a target that validates nothing, bypassed nothing. There is no second parser in this stack and no refusal to get past, so a High finding about it is a claim the scan cannot support.

judgement: Closed. The check reported a bypass whenever the marker host came back, without first establishing that anything was refusing an unknown host, so 'Host override' - an ordinary Host header - was reported here at High. It now sends a baseline first: one well-formed request carrying this target's own host, and one carrying a host minted for the scan. An ordinary Host header turned out to be that baseline rather than a technique, and it cannot be a bypass in either direction - where an unknown host is refused it is the refusal, and where it is not, there was nothing to get past - so it left the technique list and the seven wire shapes became six. The five shapes above are unaffected: they are reported on the same evidence as before, with the baseline's answer added to the analysis, which on this target says plainly that no refusal was bypassed and that what was shown is a parser accepting a request it is required to reject.

scenarios.subject: Host Header Bypass
scenarios.question: A front-end that answers every host it does not know with 403. Does any raw shape get past it, and does the scanner report one that did not?

forbid.why: nginx refuses an unknown host and rejects the folded and duplicated shapes outright, so nothing reaches the application to be reflected.
Nothing is reflected from behind the refusal.

Every URL on this front-end answers with the same 403, so every suffix looks ignored - but an identical refusal served to everyone is not a victim's page and there is nothing in it to hand to the next requester.

judgement: Closed. The deception check asked whether a static-looking variant of the URL was served the page rather than a 404, and never whether the page was a success, so a front-end answering every URL with the same 403 satisfied that for all five variants at once. There is now a status check before the claim, and the bar is a 2xx and nothing else: an error is the same refusal for everybody and carries nothing of the victim's to hand to the next requester, and a redirect carries no page either - its empty body would compare equal to any other empty body under the tolerant comparison, which is the same way the 403 got through. Below the bar the route is reported as not assessed with the status in the reason, rather than as a pass, so this front-end is now recorded as something nobody could look at rather than something that was found safe.

scenarios.subject: Open Redirect
scenarios.question: The Host header decides where a 302 sends a browser. Does the scanner confirm it with a host minted for the scan, rather than with a hostname anyone could be redirecting to?

expect.why: Confirmation rests on a host no site could be redirecting to for its own reasons, and on a second probe that redirected the same way.
A Location on a status a browser follows is a destination, so the same evidence confirms the routing claim - under its own finding type, which cites no requirement about intermediary headers.
The folded shape reaches the redirect builder.
As above, with a tab.
This route reads the first Host header, so the injected-first pair reaches it and the other order does not - which is the distinction the pair exists to draw.

forbid.why: This route reads the first Host header only, so a marker appended second never reaches it.
Same as host-bypass-reflected: nothing was validating the host, so nothing was bypassed.

judgement: Closed by the same change as host-bypass-reflected, and this route is why it was worth closing twice over: the 'Host override' finding was a third copy of an observation already reported correctly here as a confirmed Open Redirect and a confirmed Host Header Poisoning, and it carried the highest severity of the three while describing a refusal that never happened. An ordinary Host header is now the baseline that establishes whether a refusal exists at all, not a technique that claims one was defeated, so the two findings that own this observation are the only ones that make it.

scenarios.subject: Open Redirect
scenarios.question: A 302 that always goes to one well-known destination, whatever the header says. The scanner sends that hostname among its probes. Does it report an open redirect that is not there?

forbid.why: The destination is the same when the header names somewhere else, so the header is not deciding it. A scanner that matched its own probe host against a canonical destination would report this as a finding; the free control is what stops it.

notes: Not exhaustive: this endpoint redirects off the lab network, and the response-header checks follow a redirect, so what they can assess here depends on a host that does not resolve. See posture-redirect-attribution, which is about exactly that.

scenarios.subject: CORS
scenarios.question: Any origin mirrored back, with credentials. Both halves of that are findings. Does the scanner report both?

expect.why: The origin that was sent came back in Access-Control-Allow-Origin alongside Access-Control-Allow-Credentials, which is a read of the response by any site.
'null' is what a sandboxed frame sends, and this endpoint trusts it too.

scenarios.question: One origin on an allowlist and no CORS headers for anyone else. Does the scanner report nothing?

forbid.why: Nothing is reflected.
'null' is not on the allowlist.

scenarios.subject: Web Cache Poisoning
scenarios.question: A cache with the key it ships with, in front of an application that builds links from a forwarding header. Is the poisoned copy served to a request that never sent the header?

expect.analysis_contains: served to a request that never carried the header
expect.why: The gadget needs no custom VCL: X-Forwarded-Host is not in Varnish's default key, and the back-end honours it. Confirmation is the clean request coming back with the marker in it.

notes: Not exhaustive: the cache changes what every other check sees on this target, and this scenario is about one claim. The scenarios either side of it are the controlled comparison.

scenarios.subject: Web Cache Poisoning
scenarios.stack: scanner -> varnish (header in the key) -> app
scenarios.question: The same cache with the header added to the key. The application still honours it. Does the scanner stop short of calling it poisoning?

expect.why: The header still changes the response and the finding should say so. What it must not say is that anyone else was served the result.

forbid.why: The poisoned copy is filed under its own key, so a request that never sent the header gets the clean one. This is the one line of VCL that separates a High from a Medium, and the scanner is expected to notice it.

scenarios.subject: Unkeyed Input
scenarios.stack: scanner -> nginx (key without the query string) -> app
scenarios.question: A cache that ignores the query string answers every cache-buster from one stored response. The search cannot see anything here. Does the scanner say it was blind, or does it report a clean result?

forbid.why: Nothing can be learned about a header here; a finding either way would be invented.
As above.

log_require.why: Declared because this is the property the tool leads with: a check that could not look says so instead of letting the target read as clean. The reason exists inside the check - it is what PR #37 added - and the question this asserts is whether it reaches the person reading the output.

judgement: **Not produced, and it is the most serious thing this lab found.** The search did refuse to guess: it stopped because a cache answered a URL the scan had just invented. But the reason reaches nobody. Three places were checked on this run. The console prints the banner, the progress and `No vulnerabilities were found.`, and nothing about a check that could not look. The findings file is `[]`. And the evidence report says ASVS-5.0:4.1.3 **Pass**, assessed by the four checks that did run, with `not_assessed_because: []` - 25 Pass, 1 Not assessed, and that one is the baseline requirement, not this. The string `not part of its key` appears nowhere in either artefact.

Why it happens: `skip()` records the reason on the check, and `compliance/evidence.py` reads it only for controls that end up with no assessor at all. Here three other checks also map to 4.1.3, found nothing, and carried the control to Pass - so the one check that could have found a poisoning gadget on this target drops out of the record silently. A reader of the evidence file is told the requirement was met.

This is the erosion the project's own notes name: an unassessable check falling through as a pass. It is reported and not fixed, because the fix is a change to what the evidence report promises - a control assessed by some checks and blocked for others needs a third state, or a per-check note beside the Pass - and this pull request does not touch detection or reporting logic. Reproduce it with `python lab/lab.py --only cache-blind-query-key` and read `out/cache-blind-query-key.evidence.json`.

scenarios.subject: Web Cache Deception
scenarios.question: A router that ignores a path parameter, on a page a shared cache is free to store. Does the scanner see the suffix being ignored?

expect.why: '/deception;.css' is served as '/deception', and nothing in the response forbids a shared cache from storing it. With no CDN in this stack the check is expected to stop at potential rather than claim a confirmed deception.

scenarios.subject: Response header posture
scenarios.question: This URL's own response is hardened; it redirects to one that is not. Whose response headers end up in the report, and does the report say whose they are?

expect.why: The posture check follows the redirect, and the finding names the URL it actually assessed. That part is honest, and this scenario records it rather than asserting a behaviour nobody has decided on.

judgement: Worth a decision, not a defect in detection: the findings name the URL they came from, but the evidence report's target list names the URL that was asked for, so a per-control Pass or Fail can be earned by a different response than the one an assessor thinks they are reading. A scan of a URL that redirects off-site also leaves the target, which is why this lab's network has no route anywhere. Not fixed here: changing it is a decision about the evidence report's contract, and this pull request does not touch detection logic.
